predictedRisks.riskTitle: Discovery-Phase Scope Redefinition Causes Downstream Schedule and Cost Pressure
predictedRisks.riskDescription: Because deliverables, acceptance criteria, and features may be re-defined during Discovery, the project is exposed to downstream rework, timeline slippage, and change-control pressure once architecture, design, and development begin.
predictedRisks.rootCause: Requirements and feature baseline are not yet fixed, and the SOW explicitly allows redefinition during Discovery.
triggerConditions: Discovery outputs materially change feature definitions or acceptance criteria
Additional business scenarios or line-of-business needs emerge during Discovery
Integration or security requirements are identified after initial baseline discussions
Change requests increase before architecture is finalized

potentialImpact.schedule: Architecture and development start may be delayed; downstream milestones may compress
potentialImpact.cost: Additional effort may require change requests or consume contingency implicitly
potentialImpact.quality: Late changes may increase rework and reduce design stability
potentialImpact.customer: Stakeholder confidence may reduce if baseline shifts repeatedly
potentialImpact.operations: Operational readiness planning may be delayed due to unstable scope

supportingPatterns: Discovery-phase scope fluidity tends to increase downstream change risk
Features and acceptance criteria may be updated during Discovery
Material scope changes may invoke formal change management

mitigationPlan: Lock a signed Discovery baseline for scope, integrations, and acceptance criteria before detailed build planning
Create a prioritized feature inventory by line of business with explicit in-scope/out-of-scope decisions
Use formal change control immediately after Discovery baseline approval
Track unresolved requirements and architectural assumptions as named decisions with due dates
recommendations: Establish a Discovery exit gate requiring approved requirements, integration inventory, and acceptance criteria
Limit late feature additions unless business-critical and commercially approved
Publish a decision log for open scope items and dependency assumptions
predictedRisks.reasoning: This risk is directly supported by the SOW language that deliverables and acceptance criteria may be re-defined during Discovery, combined with an aggressive six-month timeline that leaves limited tolerance for downstream rework.
monitoringIndicators: Count of features updated during Discovery
Unapproved acceptance criteria at Discovery exit
Volume of change requests before design sign-off

projectIndicators: Timeline is indicative and finalized after Discovery
Deliverables and acceptance criteria may be re-defined during Discovery
Features may be updated during Discovery phase
historicalReferences: No historical risk register IDs provided; pattern derived from baseline historical intelligence only

predictedRisks.riskTitle: Environment and Access Readiness Delays Push Development Start
predictedRisks.riskDescription: If required environments, cloud infrastructure access, security clearances, and system connectivity are not provisioned on time by the client and dependent parties, development mobilization and early sprint execution may be delayed.
predictedRisks.rootCause: Critical-path delivery prerequisites are dependent on Company provisioning of environments, access, and approvals before development can start.
triggerConditions: Development, staging, or production environments are not provisioned as planned
System access or security approvals are pending
Third-party/API access is delayed
Cloud setup dependencies remain unresolved at architecture completion

potentialImpact.schedule: Development start and sprint cadence may slip by multiple weeks
potentialImpact.cost: Team idle time or replanning may increase delivery cost pressure
potentialImpact.quality: Compressed downstream build and test windows may reduce quality assurance depth
potentialImpact.customer: Go-live confidence may reduce due to missed early milestones
potentialImpact.operations: Operational setup and release planning may become reactive

supportingPatterns: Complex multi-dependency projects create early-phase delivery fragility
Dependency delays are inherently elevated in the current project structure
Environment readiness is an explicit upstream dependency

mitigationPlan: Create a dependency tracker for environments, access, approvals, and API onboarding with owners and due dates
Escalate unresolved provisioning items through monthly and sprint governance
Confirm minimum viable non-production environments and fallback access paths
Sequence build work to start with components not blocked by external access where feasible
recommendations: Run a readiness review before Development kickoff
Set RAG status for each environment and access dependency
Secure named approvers for security/access decisions
predictedRisks.reasoning: The SOW explicitly states that cloud infrastructure, environments, access, and approvals are Company dependencies. At pre-Discovery stage there is no evidence these prerequisites are ready, so this is a near-term and actionable future risk.

projectIndicators: Cloud infrastructure and necessary environments must be provided before development
Company dependencies include environment provisioning, system access, security clearances, and timely approvals
Operational progress cannot be confirmed because no WSR is available
historicalReferences: No historical risk register IDs provided; baseline pattern indicates high dependency-delay recurrence exposure

predictedRisks.riskTitle: Incomplete Integration Inventory During Discovery Leads to Rework or Change Requests
predictedRisks.riskDescription: Because third-party system links and integrations are identified during Discovery and integrations not identified then are out of scope, late discovery of integration needs may create rework, delivery gaps, or formal scope change requests.
predictedRisks.rootCause: Integration scope is not fully fixed at project start, while multiple business capabilities depend on OKTA and third-party systems across several lines of business.
triggerConditions: New integration endpoints or systems are identified after Discovery
Business workflows require data or services not included in initial architecture
API documentation or vendor onboarding reveals unplanned complexity
LOB-specific portal functions require additional external dependencies

potentialImpact.schedule: Architecture revisions and build rework may delay planned sprints and testing
potentialImpact.cost: Additional integration effort may require change requests and vendor coordination
potentialImpact.quality: Late integration design may increase defects and interface instability
potentialImpact.customer: Portal functionality may not meet expected business workflows at UAT
potentialImpact.operations: Support model and operational monitoring may be incomplete for newly discovered interfaces

supportingPatterns: Integration scope unknowns discovered late can trigger rework or change requests
Integrations not identified during Discovery are out of scope

mitigationPlan: Produce a complete integration inventory during Discovery including owners, interfaces, authentication, SLAs, and test dependencies
Validate each line-of-business workflow against required external systems
Obtain vendor/API documentation and access early
Baseline interface scope and send unresolved integrations through formal change control
recommendations: Conduct integration workshops with business, architecture, security, and external system owners
Map every key feature to required upstream/downstream systems
Track unidentified integrations as top-tier Discovery risks until closed
predictedRisks.reasoning: This risk is strongly supported by the SOW’s explicit language that integrations are identified during Discovery and that unidentified integrations are out of scope, creating a predictable exposure to late discovery and rework.
monitoringIndicators: Number of features lacking mapped system dependencies
Late integration discoveries after Discovery sign-off

projectIndicators: Third-party system integration is included 'as identified'
Integrations not identified during Discovery are out of scope
Key features depend on OKTA, Insight Reporter, Benefitfocus, and other third-party links
historicalReferences: No historical risk register IDs provided; enterprise baseline pattern indicates high relevance

predictedRisks.riskTitle: Compressed End-to-End Timeline Creates Testing, UAT, and Go-Live Compression
predictedRisks.riskDescription: The six-month term covers Discovery, Architecture, Design, Development, multiple testing types, UAT, deployment, and hypercare. Any early-phase slippage is likely to compress later quality, UAT, and release activities.
predictedRisks.rootCause: The project scope is broad relative to the available duration, and the schedule is still indicative until Discovery completion.
triggerConditions: Discovery or architecture takes longer than planned
Development sprints slip due to dependencies or scope change
Testing environments or test data are not ready when needed
Defect remediation continues into planned UAT window

potentialImpact.schedule: Testing, UAT, and go-live dates may compress or slip beyond baseline end date
potentialImpact.cost: Extended effort or additional support may increase budget pressure
potentialImpact.quality: Reduced regression, performance, security, or accessibility coverage may occur under time pressure
potentialImpact.customer: Business readiness and stakeholder confidence may be affected by unstable release timing
potentialImpact.operations: Hypercare may overlap contract end or require extension planning

supportingPatterns: Aggressive end-to-end timelines increase probability of testing, UAT, and go-live compression
Full lifecycle including hypercare must fit within Mar 1 to Aug 31, 2026 baseline
Hypercare may extend beyond contract term if go-live is late August

mitigationPlan: Establish milestone buffer management from Discovery onward
Track earned progress against phase exit criteria weekly once execution begins
Start test planning, environment readiness, and UAT preparation early rather than sequentially
Define minimum acceptable quality gates that cannot be waived without executive approval
recommendations: Rebaseline timeline immediately after Discovery with explicit contingency
Protect testing and UAT windows from upstream scope leakage
Escalate any milestone drift as soon as critical path impact appears
predictedRisks.reasoning: The current baseline shows a complex multi-LOB implementation in a short delivery window with no confirmed operational progress data. This makes schedule compression risk one of the most material future risks.

projectIndicators: Timeline is indicative until Discovery completes
Hypercare may extend beyond contract end if go-live is late August
historicalReferences: No historical risk register IDs provided; baseline historical intelligence highlights schedule compression as highly relevant

predictedRisks.riskTitle: Business SME and UAT Stakeholder Availability Becomes a Critical Path Constraint
predictedRisks.riskDescription: The project depends on timely participation from Company SMEs, Product Owner/Business Lead, approvers, and UAT stakeholders. If those stakeholders are not consistently available, requirements clarification, approvals, and acceptance may be delayed.
predictedRisks.rootCause: Key client-side roles are required for decision-making, reviews, and testing, but availability is an external dependency rather than a controlled delivery resource.
triggerConditions: SME workshops are repeatedly rescheduled
Product Owner decisions are delayed
Deliverable approvals exceed review periods
UAT participants are not named or not available when testing begins

potentialImpact.schedule: Discovery decisions, design approvals, and UAT completion may slip
potentialImpact.cost: Project team may incur inefficiency from waiting or repeated walkthroughs
potentialImpact.quality: Unresolved business decisions may lead to assumptions and rework
potentialImpact.customer: Acceptance disputes may rise if stakeholders engage too late
potentialImpact.operations: Operational readiness and training may be delayed due to late business sign-off

supportingPatterns: Dependency delays are inherently elevated due to client-side approvals and SME needs
Testing and UAT readiness remain externally dependent
Multi-stakeholder enterprise programs commonly experience approval bottlenecks

mitigationPlan: Nominate named SMEs, Product Owner, approvers, and UAT leads with capacity commitments
Publish a decision calendar aligned to Discovery, design, and UAT gates
Escalate missed stakeholder commitments through governance forums
Prepare pre-read materials and rapid decision logs to reduce meeting burden
recommendations: Secure executive confirmation of stakeholder availability before Discovery begins
Track approval aging and workshop attendance as formal delivery KPIs
Define backup approvers and alternate UAT participants
predictedRisks.reasoning: The SOW repeatedly identifies stakeholder availability, approvals, and UAT participation as client responsibilities. In a compressed timeline, these dependencies are highly material and phase-specific.

projectIndicators: Company must provide SME access, approvals, Product Owner/Business Lead, and UAT stakeholders
Deliverable reviews and sign-offs are client dependencies
No WSR evidence exists to confirm current stakeholder mobilization
historicalReferences: No historical risk register IDs provided; baseline historical intelligence identifies resource availability as a relevant risk theme

predictedRisks.riskTitle: Late Security, Compliance, and Data Governance Inputs Cause Design Rework
predictedRisks.riskDescription: If security policies, compliance requirements, RBAC rules, or data governance constraints are provided late or incompletely during Discovery, architecture and design decisions may need rework and downstream testing effort may increase.
predictedRisks.rootCause: Critical control requirements are expected to be shared during Discovery rather than already fixed at project initiation.
triggerConditions: Security requirements are incomplete at architecture review
RBAC or identity-management rules change after design sign-off
Compliance controls emerge after development has started
Data handling constraints affect integration or database design late

potentialImpact.schedule: Architecture, development, and security testing may be delayed by redesign and remediation
potentialImpact.cost: Additional implementation and retesting effort may be required
potentialImpact.quality: Late control changes can increase defect density and weaken early design cohesion
potentialImpact.customer: User experience or access model may change late in the cycle
potentialImpact.operations: Production readiness and auditability may be affected

supportingPatterns: Requirements and scope ambiguity early in lifecycle create downstream rework
Identity and access dependencies are central to this portal implementation
Compliance and data governance are explicitly expected during Discovery

mitigationPlan: Engage security, compliance, and IAM stakeholders in Discovery workshops from project start
Baseline RBAC, SSO, data handling, and audit requirements before detailed design
Include security acceptance criteria in phase exit gates
Trace each major feature to applicable control requirements
recommendations: Run early architecture and control reviews with security stakeholders
Do not finalize solution design without approved security/compliance inputs
Plan security testing scenarios during design, not after build completion
predictedRisks.reasoning: This risk is supported by the SOW statement that security policies, compliance requirements, and data governance rules will be shared during Discovery, creating exposure if these are delayed or incomplete.
monitoringIndicators: Architecture review findings related to controls

projectIndicators: Security policies, compliance requirements, and data governance rules are to be shared during Discovery
Portal includes SSO, RBAC, and producer data features
Testing strategy includes security and NFR validation
historicalReferences: No historical risk register IDs provided; risk enriched from baseline historical themes only
